strengths: Novel physics-informed graph representation: The paper presents an elegant way to encode physical laws (such as building shading, vegetation evapotranspiration, and wind-driven convective diffusion) directly into the topology of a dynamic heterogeneous graph, which is highly intuitive and effective.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The authors compare UrbanGraph against a diverse set of baseline models spanning multiple paradigms, including grid-based CNN models (CGAN-LSTM), homogeneous GNNs (GCN, GINE), generative graph models (GAE, GGAN), and various temporal models (GRU, Transformer).

Extensive ablation studies: The paper includes a very thorough set of ablations in the main text and appendix, validating almost every design choice (including the heterogeneous graph mechanism, the dynamic mechanism, specific edge types, global-spatial feature fusion strategies, the warming-up mechanism, and the prediction head architecture).

Release of a high-resolution benchmark dataset: The construction and release of the UMC4/12 dataset (based on ENVI-met simulations of Singapore) is a valuable contribution to the urban computing and spatio-temporal modeling communities.

High-quality writing and presentation: The paper is exceptionally clear, logically organized, and accompanied by informative visualizations and details of both the physical and neural network components.
weaknesses: Evaluation limited to simulated data: The dataset used for evaluation is entirely simulated via the ENVI-met numerical model. While ENVI-met is standard, real-world urban environments have unmodeled complexities (e.g., anthropogenic heat from traffic and AC, sensor noise). The paper lacks validation on real-world observational data.

Lack of analysis on graph construction overhead: Although the paper notes that UrbanGraph is computationally efficient (in FLOPs) compared to baselines, it does not clearly quantify the computational overhead of constructing the dynamic heterogeneous graphs (e.g., calculating shadow lengths, vegetation activity radius, and effective wind distances) at each timestep. If this preprocessing is slow, it could impact real-time deployment.

Sensitivity to physical hyperparameters: The dynamic edge construction relies on several manually set physical parameters (e.g., wind effect coefficient \lambda_{wind}, shadow angle width \Delta\phi_{shadow}, base radius R_{base}). While the choices are physically motivated, a sensitivity analysis on these parameters would help understand the robustness of the graph representation.

strengths: A novel and highly practical physics-informed graph representation that embeds time-varying physical processes (shading, evapotranspiration, convective diffusion) directly into the topology of a dynamic heterogeneous graph, serving as a clean 'observational bias'.

The introduction and public release of the UMC4/12 benchmark dataset, generated from high-fidelity 3D microclimate simulations (ENVI-met) using real-world GIS data, which provides a valuable resource for the spatio-temporal modeling community.
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation with strong results, outperforming multiple competitive baselines in both prediction accuracy and computational efficiency.
Extensive ablation studies and sensitivity analyses (e.g., validating the importance of each edge type, dynamic vs. static, heterogeneous vs. homogeneous, fusion mechanisms, and warming-up schemes).
Excellent visual results and detailed documentation of physical parameters and simulation settings in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The dynamic graph construction relies on knowing exact real-time physical variables (e.g., wind speed, wind direction, global radiation) at future timesteps. In practice, these are forecast variables that carry uncertainty; the paper does not analyze the model's robustness to noisy or uncertain environmental inputs.

The core deep learning architecture is relatively standard, combining existing building blocks (RGCN and LSTM). The primary novelty is centered on the domain-specific graph construction rather than architectural breakthroughs.

The evaluation is geographically constrained to Singapore (a tropical climate). The generalizability of the proposed edge-construction heuristics to temperate, arid, or cold climates is not demonstrated.

strengths: The paper is very well-structured, clear, and accompanied by a detailed appendix containing extensive experimental results, hyperparameter choices, and visualizations.
The concept of converting physical processes (such as shading, wind direction, and vegetation evapotranspiration) into dynamic edges in a heterogeneous graph is intuitive and physically motivated.
The paper performs a wide range of ablation studies covering spatial/temporal fusion strategies, prediction head architectures, and individual edge types.
weaknesses: Extremely limited dataset diversity: The entire UMC4/12 dataset is generated from a simulation of only one single extreme heat day in Singapore. Because Singapore is tropical and has very little seasonal variation, evaluating on a single day means the model's ability to generalize to different weather conditions, seasons, or geographical regions is unproven and likely highly limited.

Lack of real-world validation: The evaluation is conducted entirely on simulated data from ENVI-met. There is no comparison or validation against real-world urban meteorological sensor measurements, which leaves the practical utility of the proposed method unclear.

Limited machine learning novelty: The core model architecture is a relatively standard combination of Relational Graph Convolutional Networks (RGCN, 2017) and LSTM. The main novelty lies in the manual heuristic rules used to construct the dynamic edges (Equations 3-7). These rules rely on simplified, hard-thresholded binary relations (e.g., shadow length, wind-alignment distance), which may not capture the complex, continuous non-linear physical interactions.

Weak spatio-temporal baselines: The comparison relies on very basic baseline configurations (e.g., GCN-LSTM, GINE-LSTM). The authors do not compare against state-of-the-art spatio-temporal GNNs (e.g., Graph WaveNet, AGCRN, DCRNN) or standard surrogate architectures for physical field modeling (e.g., Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) or U-Net-based neural operators).

Poor performance on dynamic variables: While the model achieves high R² scores on UTCI and PET (which are highly dependent on Mean Radiant Temperature/shading), Table A12 reveals that the performance on core dynamic variables like Air Temperature (0.5650) and Relative Humidity (0.5159) is quite low. This indicates that the heuristic graph struggles to capture the actual convective and fluid dynamics of the microclimate.

Inconsistent evaluation settings: There is an awkward discrepancy in model configurations. The main results in Table 1 use a 128-dimensional model, whereas the ablation studies in Table 2 and the appendix use a 384-dimensional model optimized by Optuna. This inconsistency makes it difficult to assess the true relative gains of the framework and raises questions about whether all baselines were fairly and consistently tuned.

strengths: The paper introduces an innovative, physically grounded approach to constructing graph topologies, translating physical principles (shading, advection, evapotranspiration) into explicit dynamic and heterogeneous causal edges. This acts as a strong, physically consistent structural constraint.

The proposed causal pruning based on physical bounds significantly reduces the graph density, leading to a massive reduction in FLOPs (73.8% relative to LRGCN) and improved training efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.

The evaluation is exceptionally thorough, comparing against multiple classes of baselines (grid-based, static spatio-temporal GNNs, generative graphs, and dynamic graphs) across six different microclimate target variables.

The authors demonstrate strong generalization capabilities, validating their simulation dataset against real-world field sensors, city-scale datasets, and even transferring the paradigm to model fluid flow fields governed by Navier-Stokes equations.
The appendix is comprehensive, featuring extensive ablation studies on physics injection strategies, temporal modules, fusion mechanisms, prediction head architectures, and parameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: The GNN model itself is trained and evaluated on simulated data (ENVI-met and OpenFOAM). Although the simulators are validated with real measurements, directly evaluating the model's prediction accuracy on a dense network of real-world sensor observations (independent of a simulator) would further strengthen the practical claims.

The construction of the physics-informed edges relies on several heuristic thresholds and parameters (e.g., maximum shadow extent, wind effect coefficient) sourced from literature. Although sensitivity analysis is provided, calibrating these parameters automatically for different climates/regions remains an open challenge.

The core architectural components (RGCN and LSTM) are standard; the novelty is primarily concentrated in the heuristic-driven physical graph construction phase rather than new neural network operators.

strengths: Innovative Framework: UrbanGraph introduces a novel way of incorporating physical laws (such as solar shading, vegetation evapotranspiration, and wind-modulated convection) as hard topological constraints in a dynamic, heterogeneous graph. This is a refreshing alternative to standard Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) that rely on computationally expensive soft PDE loss terms.

Superior Performance and Efficiency: The model outperforms multiple state-of-the-art baselines (including grid-based, static graph, generative graph, and dynamic graph models) in terms of R2, RMSE, and MAE. Remarkably, it achieves a massive reduction in FLOPs (73.8%) and a 21% reduction in training time compared to implicit recurrent graph baselines like LRGCN.

Robust Empirical Validation: The authors perform exceptionally rigorous validation, including evaluation on a newly introduced high-resolution dataset (UMC4/12), real-world validation against physical sensors in Singapore, city-scale validation using the HiGTS dataset, and generalizability to a completely different physical domain (3D fluid dynamics) using the UWF3D dataset governed by Navier-Stokes equations.

Thorough Ablation Studies: The appendix contains detailed ablation studies dissecting the contribution of each edge type, the physics injection strategy, temporal modules, fusion mechanisms, and multi-task vs. single-task learning setups.

Open Science Commitment: The authors' commitment to releasing both the codebase and the high-resolution UMC4/12 dataset is a valuable contribution that will facilitate future research in urban computing and climate resilience.
weaknesses: Sensitivity to Meteorological Noise: Since the graph's dynamic edges are explicitly constructed based on hourly wind speed, wind direction, solar radiation, and solar position, the model's accuracy could be sensitive to noise or errors in the input meteorological forecasts. A robustness study examining how input weather noise propagates to the final predictions would strengthen the evaluation.

Reliance on Domain-Expert Heuristics: The threshold parameters used to construct the dynamic edges (e.g., shadow lengths, influence radii, wind modulation factors) are manually selected from urban climatology literature. Tuning these thresholds for new regions or different resolutions might require substantial domain-specific engineering, limiting immediate out-of-the-box usage by non-experts.

Graph Reconstruction Overhead at Scale: Although the authors provide a city-scale stress test in the appendix, reconstructing the heterogeneous adjacency matrices at every timestep can scale quadratically in the worst case. Moving some of the scalability and spatial indexing discussion from the appendix to the main text would help address concerns regarding practical real-time execution.

strengths: The paper targets a highly relevant and challenging problem of urban microclimate prediction, which is computationally expensive when using traditional CFD or numerical simulations.
The authors generated and plan to release two high-resolution spatio-temporal datasets (UMC4/12 and UWF3D), which could serve as valuable resources for the research community.
The paper provides extensive ablation analyses in the appendix, exploring different edge configurations, fusion strategies, and temporal models.
weaknesses: The core architecture relies on standard, off-the-shelf components, specifically a standard Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN) and a standard LSTM. The main contribution is the 'physics-informed' topology, which is constructed using hand-crafted, rule-based heuristics rather than a novel learnable representation or a mathematically integrated physical prior (such as neural operators or differentiable physics).

The proposed topological reconstruction rules introduce numerous physical hyperparameters (e.g., maximum shadow extent, base radius of influence, wind effect coefficient, etc.). This heavy reliance on manual parameter engineering makes it difficult to generalize the model to different cities (with varying latitudes, morphologies, or wind climates) without significant manual recalibration.

The model is trained and evaluated purely on simulated datasets (ENVI-met and OpenFOAM). While simulating physical systems is standard, it makes the model a surrogate of a simulator rather than a direct predictor of real-world microclimates. Although Appendix B.2 shows validation of the ENVI-met simulator itself against weather stations, there is a lack of direct evaluation of the machine learning model's predictions against real-world observational data.

The claim of 'up to 10.8% improvement in R²' is calculated relative to the weakest grid-based baseline (CGAN-LSTM). However, when compared to stronger and simpler graph baselines such as GAE-LSTM (R² = 0.8494), the improvement of UrbanGraph (R² = 0.8542) is very marginal (<0.6% in R²). This small performance gain may not justify the high computational and design complexity of dynamically constructing 5 distinct heterogeneous edge types at each timestep.

The compared models are mostly generic traffic forecasting spatio-temporal GNNs (e.g., STGCN, ASTGCN). The paper lacks comparisons against modern physics-informed ML architectures and neural operators (e.g., Fourier Neural Operators, DeepONet, or MeshGraphNets) which are the state-of-the-art for physical field modeling.

The manuscript contains several typographical errors and incomplete placeholder sentences. For instance, in Appendix B.2.1, it reads: 'We conducted a rigorous validation of the ENVI-met model based on a sensor network deployed on the campus of the .' (leaving the name of the campus blank and ending with a dangling period). There are also missing spaces before citations/sentences (e.g., 'efficiency(Heo et al.)' on page 2, 'environments.While' on page 3, 'interactions.Comprehensive' on page 2) and an incomplete citation reference for 'Xue;' on page 3.
